parts.note: the Greek warrior of myth whose one weak spot was his heel, where Paris's arrow struck him

explanation.surface: A remark about some legendary champion having a weakness.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the Trojan War hero dipped in the Styx by his mother, unprotected only at the heel she held.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iliad's greatest Greek warrior was invulnerable save for the heel, so he is the legendary hero with one vulnerable spot.

explanation.surface: A Cockney asks whether something is offhand, like Esau.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves drop the H Cockney-style: offhand becomes 'off-'and', and hairy, as Esau was in Genesis, becomes 'airy.
explanation.definitionFit: Airy means casual or nonchalant, as an offhand manner is; Esau was a hairy man, which with the H dropped sounds the same.

clue.text: Robust farm animal has quarters in Worcestershire

parts.note: hale means healthy and robust
a sow is a female pig
E and N, east and north, are two of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: A sturdy beast on a farm has lodgings in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarters' looks like lodgings but gives two compass points. Halesowen was a town in Worcestershire, an English Midlands county.
explanation.definitionFit: Halesowen is a town near Birmingham historically within Worcestershire, so it lies in that county.

explanation.surface: Someone thrashes away at a cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lid' reads as a cover but is an eyelid.
explanation.definitionFit: To lash is to whip, so lashes are beats; eyelashes grow on the eyelid.

clue.text: Cure disorder without trouble in South America

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the jumbled word goes round the trouble
disorder tells us the letters of cure are thrown into a new order

parts.note: ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Fix an illness without any fuss somewhere in South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking: ECUR, the anagram of CURE, goes around ADO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecuador is a republic on the Pacific coast of South America.

clue.text: Jacobson put in appearance in Morocco

indicators.note: put in tells us one piece is placed inside the word for appearance

parts.note: an air is a manner or appearance someone gives off
Gad was one of the twelve sons of Jacob in Genesis, so a Jacob son

explanation.surface: Someone called Jacobson turns up in North Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jacobson' reads as a surname but splits as Jacob's son, GAD, which goes inside AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Agadir is a port city on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, so it is a place found in that country.

indicators.note: cooks suggests the letters are worked up into a different form, like food prepared

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone prepares an uncooked drumstick from a fowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooks' is the anagram signal on RAW LEG OF; the great auk was once called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The garefowl is an old name for the great auk, an extinct flightless seabird.

explanation.surface: Note down a book of the Old Testament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Book of Samuel' suggests the Bible, but it is Samuel Pepys's famous journal of 1660s London.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily journal is a record of events; Samuel Pepys's best-known book is his journal.

explanation.surface: An amusing topic of conversation, namely eating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diverting' suggests amusing, but a red herring diverts attention from the real issue.
explanation.definitionFit: A false lead that distracts attention shares its name with a smoked, reddened fish eaten as food.

clue.text: Dandy with some woad on, I suppose !

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A fop wearing a bit of blue body paint, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: Woad is the blue dye ancient Britons painted themselves with.
explanation.definitionFit: An adonis is a strikingly handsome young man, and so a dandy or beau.

indicators.note: words that are sound here means said aloud, so we hear a word for parts

parts.note: an actor's parts are roles

explanation.surface: Lists of components that are in good working order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like 'healthy', but it signals a homophone: ROLES heard aloud gives the spelling for lists.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolls are official registers or lists of names, as in electoral rolls.

explanation.surface: Clandestine work, maybe for the secret service.
explanation.walkthrough: In tennis an underhand serve is delivered with the arm below the shoulder; 'Secret service' looks like one phrase but splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Underhand dealings are sly and concealed; a serve with the hand below shoulder level is an underhand delivery.

clue.text: Grey is going to study Maugham's book

parts.note: ashen means grey or pale in colour
a den is a private study or work room

explanation.surface: Someone named Grey plans to study a novel by Maugham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grey' looks like a person's name, but it is a colour; 'is going to' merely links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerset Maugham's 1928 collection of spy stories is titled after its agent hero, Ashenden.

clue.text: City of backward type by river

indicators.note: something of a backward type runs the wrong way, so the joined pieces are read in reverse

parts.note: Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
taken as written

explanation.surface: A town of a regressive sort standing beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY then OF, read backwards, gives the river; ELY is the cathedral city in the English fens.
explanation.definitionFit: The Foyle is a river in Ireland flowing past Londonderry into Lough Foyle.

clue.text: So I must be a temperate sort ?

indicators.note: sort is read as a verb, telling us to arrange the preceding letters

explanation.surface: A speaker reckons they must be a moderate type of person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort' looks like a noun meaning kind, but it is the anagram signal on SO I MUST BE A.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstemious means moderate and sparing in eating and drinking, as a temperate person is.

explanation.surface: Seize control of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bowler delivers an over of six balls, so to take the over is to bowl; 'Take over' reads as seizing control.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket one bowls an over, a set of six deliveries; a bowl is also a round dish or container.

parts.note: both the potable stuff from rivers and lakes, and a town of that name on the Isle of Wight

explanation.surface: A question about the local drink on the Isle of Wight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Wight (I.O.W.) is an island off England's south coast with a village called Freshwater; 'drunk' suggests alcohol but means drinkable water.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsalted water is what people drink, and a village of that name lies on the Isle of Wight.

indicators.note: in a down clue put up means the word is written upwards, so read in reverse

parts.note: an Ave is a Hail Mary prayer

explanation.surface: A young woman offered up a prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: AVE written upwards in the grid gives the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Eva is a girl's given name.

explanation.surface: A role in a stage drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a role in a drama, but means an alphabet symbol; the play is Maugham's 1927 drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Any symbol of the alphabet is a character; Somerset Maugham wrote a stage drama with this title.

indicators.note: after puts the drink behind the numerals

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
L is fifty in Roman numerals
lager is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A resident has a beer after ten to seven.
explanation.walkthrough: '6 : 50' looks like a time, but it is two Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: A villager is a resident of a village, so an inhabitant.

parts.note: the thing hit back and forth on a tennis court, not the subject of a lawsuit

explanation.surface: The subject of a lawsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court action' suggests legal proceedings; the court is a tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: On a tennis court play centres on the felt-covered sphere struck by the players' rackets.

parts.note: twig brooms used for sweeping, whose name is also slang for slovenly women

explanation.surface: Untidy charwomen.
explanation.walkthrough: A besom is a broom of twigs, and in dialect also a slattern.
explanation.definitionFit: Besoms are brooms for sweeping, and the word also means slovenly women.

indicators.note: letters suggests the characters of these words are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman is mentioned in a duke's correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letters' reads as correspondence but means the letters of IN DUCAL rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucinda is a girl's given name.

clue.text: It provides some guiding rule for a speaker

indicators.note: for a speaker means as it is heard when said aloud

parts.note: a reign is a monarch's rule

explanation.surface: Something giving a public speaker a guiding principle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rule for a speaker' looks like a guideline for orators; it is REIGN as heard aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: A strap held by a rider steers a horse, so it supplies some of the guidance.

explanation.surface: Home ground and the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is Shakespeare's tragedy of the Danish prince.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamlet is a small village where people dwell; it is also Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: Good finish to a royal castle

indicators.note: only the finishing part of the castle's name is wanted, so its opening is dropped

parts.note: Balmoral is the British royal family's castle in Scotland

explanation.surface: A fine ending to a visit to a palace.
explanation.walkthrough: BALMORAL is the Scottish home of the British royals; its finish, with BAL removed, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Moral behaviour is ethically right, so a moral person is a good one.

clue.text: Cook writes nonsense about a Pole

indicators.note: about places the nonsense around the following pieces

parts.note: rot is rubbish or nonsense
S, south, is one of the two poles

explanation.surface: A chef writes rubbish about a Polish person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person but is the South Pole, S; ROT goes about A and S.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast is to cook in an oven or over a fire.

clue.text: Urgent message about case of philosopher

indicators.note: about places the distress signal round the word for case

parts.note: SOS is the international distress signal
a crate is a packing case

explanation.surface: A distress call concerning a packing case belonging to a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: SOS is split to go around CRATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Socrates was the Athenian thinker who taught Plato.

clue.text: A pressing matter for a visitor

definitions.text: A pressing matter for a visitor

parts.words: A pressing matter for a visitor
parts.note: the thing a caller presses at the front door to announce arrival

explanation.surface: An urgent issue facing a guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pressing' suggests urgent; it means pushed with a finger.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorbell is pushed by someone arriving at a house.

parts.note: a member of an Ulster loyalist order; read as a figure shot from 0 range, nil distance being point-blank

explanation.surface: News of a Protestant killed at close quarters.
explanation.walkthrough: Point-blank range is zero range: O RANGE, and the person shot is a MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orange Order is a Protestant fraternal society in Northern Ireland, whose members carry its colour's name.

parts.note: the underworld stream whose water brings forgetfulness, which elephants, who never forget, would avoid

explanation.surface: A river that elephants stay away from.
explanation.walkthrough: Proverbially an elephant never forgets, so it would avoid the river of oblivion in Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the dead drank from this underworld stream to forget their earthly lives.

clue.text: Tries a variety of literary work

indicators.note: a variety of means the letters come in a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone attempts several kinds of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIES with A (from 'a variety') is rearranged; 'a' does double service in the surface but the fodder is TRIES plus the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire is a genre of writing that mocks folly through irony and ridicule.

parts.note: bygone means past
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A poem set as a question in an old exam paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set in' joins the definition to the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastoral is a poem idealising rural life and shepherds.
